name: Harbor Gateway Tower

gallery.caption: Core slipform running ahead of the steel
Moment frame bolt-up, nineteen floors up

blurb: A 32-storey office tower on reclaimed harbour ground, framed to ride a magnitude 7 event with its core intact.
overview: Harbor Gateway sits on reclaimed ground half a mile from the fault trace, which put seismic demand, not gravity, in charge of every member size. We ran a buckling-restrained braced frame against a full non-linear time history, tuned the core wall to take the drift, and drove the foundations through liquefiable fill to competent material. The tower was built over an operating parking structure that never closed.

name: Katella Medical Pavilion

gallery.caption: Night pour beside the occupied wing
Central plant tied in across four windows

blurb: An outpatient pavilion built hard against a working hospital, with the acute wing running the whole time.
overview: The pavilion shares a wall, a plant room and an emergency vehicle route with a hospital that could not lose a single bed. Noise, vibration and infection control governed the programme more than the structure did: heavy work ran nights, the tie-in to the central plant was staged across four two-hour windows, and every penetration was sealed and pressure-tested before the shift ended.

name: Civic Center Seismic Retrofit

gallery.caption: New shear wall reinforcement before the pour
Steel collar fixed to the 1968 frame

blurb: A 1968 concrete frame strengthened to current code and given two more floors, with staff at their desks throughout.
overview: The existing frame had capacity nobody had ever calculated, so we started with a laser scan, core samples and a load test rather than an assumption. Strengthening was targeted at fourteen columns and two transfer beams, which was enough to carry the new floors and the code-level drift without touching the occupied levels. Work ran floor by floor behind temporary partitions.

name: Carson Tank Farm Rebuild

gallery.caption: Shell seam welding under cover
Ground improvement before the ring wall

blurb: Four API 650 tanks, their containment and the manifold that ties them in, built inside a terminal that never stopped shipping.
overview: Two tanks came down and four went up on the same footprint, with the terminal loading trucks through the whole programme. Ring wall foundations were designed for liquefiable fill with stone columns beneath; shells were built by the shell-jacking method to keep the welding at ground level. Every seam was vacuum-box and radiograph tested, and the manifold was hydrotested before the first tie-in was cut.

name: El Segundo Hydrotreater Revamp

gallery.caption: The rack, mid-turnaround
Spool fit-up under a weld tent

blurb: A capacity revamp with 38 tie-ins into live systems, executed inside an eleven-day turnaround window.
overview: The revamp needed 38 cuts into systems that could only be opened during the annual turnaround. Every spool was fabricated, tested and laid down in erection order before the unit came off line, each tie-in was rehearsed against the scan-registered model, and the sequence was written so no two cuts competed for the same crane. The unit came back on specification on the first pass.

name: Beacon Offshore Tieback

gallery.caption: Saturation bell on the moon pool
Habitat welding on the riser clamp

blurb: A subsea tieback and riser clamp repair at 412 feet, welded dry inside a habitat by a saturation dive team.
overview: Inspection found fatigue cracking in two riser clamps on a fixed platform, in water too deep and too cold for a wet weld to meet the class. We designed the repair around a welding habitat: the clamp was dewatered, preheated and welded dry, to AWS D3.6M class A, by a saturation team living at depth for eighteen days. Every pass was video-logged and ultrasonically verified before the habitat came off.

facts.v: AWS D3.6M class A, dry habitat

name: Pier J Berth Deepening

gallery.caption: Pile jacket checked before grouting
Dive control on the barge alongside

blurb: Deepening a container berth and repairing 214 piles underneath it, without taking the berth out of service.
overview: Dredging to take post-panamax draft undermined the existing pile embedment, so every pile in the affected bay needed a jacket and a structural weld before the dredger could pass. Dive crews worked surface-supplied between vessel calls, welding wet to class B where the repair allowed and setting habitats where it did not. The berth handled ships through the entire programme.

name: Terminal Island Wharf Strengthening

gallery.caption: Crane rail works along the live berth
Dive spread set for the pile jackets

blurb: A 1970s wharf brought up to carry the next generation of ship-to-shore cranes, with the underdeck repaired by divers.
overview: The terminal wanted cranes 2.4 times heavier than the wharf was built for. A full underdeck survey, half of it by dive team, found chloride damage worse at the splash zone than the records suggested. We designed a new crane beam carried on supplemental piles, jacketed the worst of the existing ones, and sequenced the work so no more than one crane rail was ever out of service.

name: Catalina Channel Outfall Repair

gallery.caption: Survey spread on the support vessel
Diver on the repaired section

blurb: A damaged subsea outfall located, clamped and welded in place, with the discharge never taken off line.
overview: A dropped anchor had dented and cracked a section of outfall in 90 feet of water. We surveyed the full run by ROV, designed a split clamp that could be set and welded by divers against a live flow, and installed it in four dive days. Post-repair ultrasonic testing and a pressure survey confirmed the line back to full rated flow.

facts.v: Split clamp, wet weld class B

name: Santa Ana River Bridge Replacement

gallery.caption: Falsework and rebar before the deck pour
Abutment works from the levee road

blurb: A three-span replacement crossing built over a flood control channel that has to stay clear through storm season.
overview: The existing crossing was scour-critical and two lanes short. The replacement is a three-span prestressed girder bridge on drilled shafts set back from the channel, so nothing new stands in the waterway. Falsework had to be out of the channel before each storm season, which set the pour sequence, and traffic stayed on the old structure until the new one carried load.

name: Sierra Dam Outlet Works

gallery.caption: Intake trash rack welded in place
Gate frame assembled before it went in

blurb: New outlet works and gates for a 1950s dam, with the reservoir kept in service and the low-level intake welded underwater.
overview: The agency needed a controlled release capacity the original works could not deliver, and could not draw the reservoir down to build it. We staged the work behind a cofferdam, cut and lined a new low-level outlet, and had dive crews weld and seal the intake trash rack and guide frames in place. Gates were dry-commissioned before the cofferdam came out.

name: Imperial Valley Substation

gallery.caption: Transformer set on its foundation
Drilled piers below the active zone

blurb: A 500 kV switchyard on expansive desert soils, tied into a line that stays energised.
overview: The site sits on soils that swell and shrink through a 40 degree annual range, which rules out shallow pads for equipment that cannot tolerate differential movement. Every structure is on drilled piers below the active zone. Steel was galvanised and match-marked in the shop so the yard crew never waited on a fit-up, and energisation was staged bay by bay against a line that could not be dropped.
